extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in research integrity (researchers, editors, and publishing professionals)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples about how journals and publishers assess alleged plagiarism, investigate overlaps, and decide whether and when to retract published articles. Covers reporting routes, investigatory standards (e.g., COPE), author cooperation, and reputational/impact considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of insufficiently attributed text reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: "Given the extent of the insufficiently attributed text reuse this article is being retracted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree/extent of copied text without appropriate attribution is a primary ground for retraction; large or extensive overlap supports retraction. Example: the retraction notice explicitly cites the extent of insufficient attribution as the reason for retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of intention to deceive
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the reused text indicates an intention to deceive readers (versus poor referencing practices) affects the publisher's response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may review past referencing in light of current policy and judge whether there was intent to deceive. Example: for a 2007 mini-review, Karger concluded referencing was not in line with current policy but did not believe there was intent to deceive, influencing their decision not to retract that paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of COPE flowchart and formal investigation procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations into overlap should follow established procedures such as the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) flowchart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers' ethics teams should open investigations following relevant COPE guidance. Example: Karger's ethics team, established in 2021, "immediately opened an investigation for both cases of the overlap, following the relevant COPE flowchart."

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual review against journal policy at time of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns should be reviewed in the context of the journal’s instructions and plagiarism policy that applied when the article was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical policies may differ from current ones; assessments should consider what policy and norms applied at publication time. Example: Karger reviewed concerns in the context of the journal's instructions on plagiarism when the article was published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author responsiveness and cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the author responds to requests for comment and cooperates with inquiries affects handling of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple unsuccessful contact attempts can delay resolution; author agreement or disagreement with retraction is noted. Example: the author "did not respond to requests to comment... despite multiple attempts of contact," though he later agreed with the retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of action and editorial follow-through
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations should be acted on in a timely manner; long delays are criticized as undermining integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays (years or decades) in investigating and retracting problematic papers can allow further citations and harm the literature and journal credibility. Example: a report in 2013 led to retraction only in 2024 — described as taking "a ridiculously long time."

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of responses across similar cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar allegations across multiple papers (even within the same journal) should be handled consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistent handling (some papers retracted quickly, others left unretracted) raises concerns. Example: of five papers reported in 2013, three were retracted the following year, one was retracted 11 years later, and one remains unretracted despite similar concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting routes and triggers for investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns may be raised directly to editors or publicly (e.g., via PubPeer); such reports can trigger publisher investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both private reports to editors and public comments (PubPeer) can prompt ethics teams to investigate. Example: the unretracted papers were brought to the publisher’s attention after Bik left comments on PubPeer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of citation impact and downstream effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which a paper has been cited and influenced the literature is relevant to the urgency and importance of corrective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highly cited problematic papers can pollute the literature and have a 'snowball effect'; publishers should consider the contamination risk when deciding response priority. Example: one of the retracted papers had 81 citations (three-quarters since 2013), and commentators noted prolonged presence undermines other papers.
